title: The Rise and Fall of Woolworth's

scenes.text: For more than a hundred years, there was one store you could find in almost every downtown in America. A bright red sign with gold letters. Wooden floors that creaked under your feet. Long counters piled with everything from thread to goldfish. And in the back, a lunch counter where you could get a grilled cheese and a cherry Coke. It was Woolworth's.
scenes.caption: WOOLWORTH'S

scenes.text: At its peak, Woolworth's was one of the biggest retailers in the world, with thousands of stores in America and around the globe. Its headquarters was the tallest building on Earth. Millions of children spent their very first allowance there. And then, in nineteen ninety-seven, the last American Woolworth's five-and-dime closed its doors.
scenes.caption: THOUSANDS OF STORES

scenes.text: So what happened? Let's tell the story of Woolworth's, from a single store in Pennsylvania to an empire, what it was like to shop there in the fifties and sixties, and how it all came to an end.
scenes.caption: THE WHOLE STORY

scenes.text: The story begins in eighteen seventy-eight, in Watertown, New York. A young clerk named Frank Winfield Woolworth worked at a dry goods store. His boss let him set up a table of odds and ends, where everything cost just five cents. It sold out almost immediately. Woolworth realized he had found something big.
scenes.caption: EVERYTHING FOR A NICKEL

scenes.text: In eighteen seventy-nine, he borrowed three hundred dollars and opened his own store, called the Great Five Cent Store, in Utica, New York. It failed within weeks. But he tried again in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and this time, he added items at ten cents. The store was a success. The five-and-dime was born.
scenes.caption: LANCASTER, 1879

scenes.text: Woolworth's idea was revolutionary. In most stores of that time, goods were kept behind the counter, and you had to ask a clerk to show them to you. Prices were often bargained over. At Woolworth's, everything was out on the counter, where customers could pick it up and look at it. And every price was clearly marked. No haggling.
scenes.query: 1900s five and dime store interior counters
scenes.caption: NO HAGGLING

scenes.text: Woolworth was also a genius at buying. Because he ordered such huge quantities, he could demand low prices from manufacturers. He traveled to Europe to buy Christmas ornaments directly from glassblowers in Germany, and he's often credited with making glass Christmas ornaments popular in America. By the nineteen hundreds, his stores sold millions of them every year.
scenes.caption: GLASS ORNAMENTS

scenes.text: Woolworth expanded fast. He opened stores in town after town, and partnered with relatives and friends who ran their own chains. In nineteen twelve, they merged into one company, the F. W. Woolworth Company, with almost six hundred stores. It was one of the largest retail companies in the world.
scenes.caption: 596 STORES

scenes.text: In nineteen thirteen, Woolworth opened his new headquarters in New York City. The Woolworth Building was fifty-seven stories high, and for sixteen years, it was the tallest building in the world. People called it the Cathedral of Commerce. And here's the amazing part. Woolworth paid for it entirely in cash, about thirteen and a half million dollars.
scenes.caption: THE CATHEDRAL OF COMMERCE

scenes.text: Woolworth himself died in nineteen nineteen. But the company kept growing. Through the twenties, thirties and forties, a Woolworth's opened in nearly every American town big enough to have a Main Street. It became as much a part of the landscape as the post office and the bank.
scenes.caption: EVERY MAIN STREET

scenes.text: During the Depression, Woolworth's became even more important. When families had almost no money, a store where things cost a nickel or a dime was a lifeline. Mothers bought thread to mend old clothes, cheap kitchenware, and small treats for the kids. The company kept growing even in the hardest years, because people still needed the basics.
scenes.caption: THROUGH THE DEPRESSION

scenes.text: So what was it like to shop at Woolworth's in the nineteen fifties? You walked in through glass doors, and the smell hit you first. Popcorn, roasted nuts, perfume, rubber and fresh-cut fabric, all mixed together. The floors were wooden and creaky. Ceiling fans turned slowly overhead.
scenes.caption: THE SMELL

scenes.text: The counters were long and divided into sections with glass panels. There were sewing notions, with thread, buttons, zippers and patterns. Kitchen gadgets. Hardware. Toys. School supplies. Greeting cards. Cosmetics, like Evening in Paris perfume in a little blue bottle. Hairnets, bobby pins and curlers.
scenes.caption: EVERYTHING ON THE COUNTER

scenes.text: There was a candy counter with dozens of glass bins, and a clerk who weighed out your candy on a scale and poured it into a white paper bag. Chocolate-covered peanuts, malted milk balls, orange slices, spice drops, licorice and nonpareils. Sold by the quarter pound.
scenes.caption: THE CANDY COUNTER

scenes.text: And there was the pet department. Goldfish swimming in tanks. Parakeets chirping in cages. Turtles in little plastic bowls with a palm tree in the middle. Hamsters. Many children got their very first pet at Woolworth's, and carried it home in a little cardboard box with holes in the lid.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST PET

scenes.text: And at Christmas, Woolworth's was magical. The store was decorated with tinsel, garland and lights. There were whole counters of ornaments, wrapping paper, ribbon and little gifts. Children with a dollar or two came in to buy presents for their parents. A bottle of perfume for Mom, and a handkerchief or a tie clip for Dad.
scenes.caption: CHRISTMAS AT WOOLWORTH'S

scenes.text: There were records too. A rack of the latest forty-fives, and sometimes a listening booth where you could hear a song before you bought it. Woolworth's sold cheap versions of the hits, recorded by studio singers, at a lower price than the original. Many kids bought their very first record there, and some didn't realize until later that it wasn't the real band.
scenes.caption: THE RECORD RACK

scenes.text: In the back, or along one side, was the lunch counter. Woolworth's was one of the biggest restaurant operators in America. Its lunch counters served millions of meals every year. The menu was simple and cheap. Grilled cheese, tuna salad, hot turkey sandwiches with gravy, BLTs, soups and pie.
scenes.caption: THE LUNCH COUNTER

scenes.text: Shoppers stopped for a cup of coffee and a slice of pie. Office workers ate a quick lunch. Mothers treated their kids to a banana split. Teenagers sat at the counter after school. For many people, a meal at the Woolworth's counter is one of their most vivid memories of downtown.
scenes.caption: A BANANA SPLIT

scenes.text: And Woolworth's was famous for its desserts. The banana split was a specialty. At some stores, there were balloons over the counter. You popped one, and a slip of paper inside told you what you'd pay for your split, anywhere from a penny to the full price. Kids loved it.
scenes.caption: POP A BALLOON

scenes.text: The waitresses were part of the experience. Many worked there for decades, and they knew the regulars by name. They wore uniforms with little white aprons, and they could balance four plates on one arm. They called you honey, refilled your coffee without asking, and slipped the kids an extra cherry on their sundae.
scenes.caption: THE WAITRESSES

scenes.text: But the Woolworth's lunch counter also has a very important place in American history. In much of the South, lunch counters were segregated. Black customers could shop in the store, but they were not allowed to sit and eat at the counter.
scenes.caption: SEGREGATED COUNTERS

scenes.text: On February first, nineteen sixty, four young Black college students sat down at the Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina. Their names were Ezell Blair Junior, Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil and David Richmond. They politely ordered coffee. They were refused service. And they stayed in their seats until the store closed.
scenes.caption: FEBRUARY 1, 1960

scenes.text: The next day, more students came. Within days, there were hundreds. The sit-ins spread across the South, to dozens of cities. By July, the Greensboro Woolworth's served its first Black customers at the counter. Today, a section of that counter is displayed at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History in Washington.
scenes.caption: THE SMITHSONIAN

scenes.text: Those four students showed incredible courage. They were heckled, threatened and had food poured on them by angry crowds. But they stayed calm and kept coming back, day after day. The sit-ins became one of the turning points of the civil rights movement, and inspired young people all over the country to take a stand.
scenes.caption: INCREDIBLE COURAGE

scenes.text: In the fifties and sixties, Woolworth's was at its peak. By the late fifties, it was celebrating its eightieth anniversary, with more than two thousand stores. It had expanded to Canada, Britain, Germany, Mexico and beyond. In Britain, Woolworths became one of the most beloved stores in the country.
scenes.caption: THE PEAK

scenes.text: The five-and-dime name was outdated by then. Prices had gone up, and many items cost a dollar or more. But the idea was the same. A little bit of everything, at prices ordinary people could afford. And for kids with a quarter in their pocket, it was still the most exciting store in town.
scenes.caption: A QUARTER IN YOUR POCKET

scenes.text: Woolworth's also had competitors, and many towns had more than one five-and-dime. There was S. S. Kresge, W. T. Grant, J. J. Newberry, McCrory's, S. H. Kress and Ben Franklin. Kress built beautiful stores with elaborate architecture. Many Main Streets had two or three of them on the same block, competing for every nickel.
scenes.caption: KRESGE, NEWBERRY AND KRESS

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty-two, Woolworth's tried something new. It opened a chain of big discount department stores called Woolco. The same year, Kresge's opened Kmart, and a man in Arkansas named Sam Walton opened his first Walmart. It was the beginning of a new era in American shopping.
scenes.caption: 1962: WOOLCO

scenes.text: That new era was the beginning of the end for the five-and-dime. Families moved to the suburbs and shopped at malls and big discount stores. Downtowns emptied. The old Woolworth's stores on Main Street, with their creaky floors and lunch counters, were left behind.
scenes.caption: THE DOWNTOWNS EMPTIED

scenes.text: Kmart grew much faster than Woolco. Walmart grew faster still. Woolco closed its American stores in nineteen eighty-three. Meanwhile, the five-and-dimes kept losing money. One by one, through the eighties and nineties, the old stores closed. Lunch counters were torn out. The red signs came down.
scenes.caption: THE RED SIGNS CAME DOWN

scenes.text: In July of nineteen ninety-seven, the company announced that it was closing its last four hundred American five-and-dime stores. After one hundred and seventeen years, Woolworth's was gone from America. Many towns held farewell gatherings. Longtime customers came for one last grilled cheese at the counter.
scenes.caption: JULY 1997

scenes.text: But here's a surprise. The company didn't disappear. It had owned a shoe store chain called Foot Locker since nineteen seventy-four. Foot Locker was growing, while the five-and-dimes were shrinking. So the company focused on athletic shoes. In nineteen ninety-eight, it dropped the Woolworth name, and in two thousand one, it took the name of its most successful chain. Today, the company that was Woolworth's is called Foot Locker.
scenes.caption: IT BECAME FOOT LOCKER

scenes.text: The Woolworth Building still stands in Lower Manhattan, more than a hundred years old, one of the most beautiful skyscrapers in the world. The old store in Greensboro is now the International Civil Rights Center and Museum. And in many small towns, you can still see the old Woolworth's building, with its name faded on the brick.
scenes.caption: THE BUILDING STILL STANDS

scenes.text: For millions of Americans, Woolworth's was more than a store. It was where you bought your first pet, your first lipstick, your mother's birthday present and your school supplies. It was where you sat at the counter with your grandmother. It was where you learned that a dime could buy something wonderful.
scenes.caption: MORE THAN A STORE

scenes.text: It was also a place where history was made, where four young men sat down and changed the country. Few stores in America can say that. Woolworth's can.
scenes.caption: WHERE HISTORY WAS MADE

scenes.text: If you remember Woolworth's, you remember the creak of the floor, the smell of popcorn, the goldfish in the tanks and the grilled cheese at the counter. It's gone now. But for a hundred years, it was a little piece of every American town.
scenes.caption: A PIECE OF EVERY TOWN

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What do you remember buying at Woolworth's? Did you ever eat at the lunch counter, or get a pet there? We read every comment. Next time, we're hitting the road on Route sixty-six in nineteen fifty-six. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID YOU BUY AT WOOLWORTH'S?
